Meeting header
Date: 2025-04-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 min
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Nina Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Sara Lopez (Acme - Head of ML), David Kim (Acme - SRE), Rita Banerjee (Acme - Product)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick off real quick. this is our weekly poc sync to go over the benchmark numbers vs your current baseline provider, cloud provider x, and talk through tuning and next steps. sara, david, thanks for making time.
[00:15] Sara: yeah thanks, maya. excited to see the numbers, we had some questions from the eng team after last week.
[00:22] Liam: hi all, i'll take the deep dive section today on the perf numbers, quick note the spreadsheet i uploaded has per-run logs, some of the runs got labeled oddly by the collector so please ignore runs with tag "test-run-0x" - those were warmup mistakes.
[00:35] David: got it, we saw that. one quick ask - can you re-export ms per token and tokens per second both at p50/p95/p99? that helps our SRE sizing.
[00:45] Liam: yep will do. quick summary here: baseline (cloudproviderx) numbers from your infra team show p50 latency ~210ms, p95 ~480ms on the 13B workload with batch size 1 under your current concurrency. our Redwood pod runs (dedicated config, medium quant) show p50 ~140ms, p95 ~320ms, tokens/sec steady-state ~1,150 versus baseline ~750. those are med-quality runs; with aggressive quantization we drop latency another ~10-15% at the expense of a small quality lift.
[01:10] Sara: that p95 diff is promising. can you explain which knobs we changed? was it batching, kernel selection, kv cache?
[01:17] Liam: yeah so three main things. 1) kernel selection/runtime optimizations - we pick conv-optimized kernels for the attention pattern you have (long context). 2) continuous batching - we allow tiny batching across requests up to 32ms window which improved gpu utilization. 3) prefix/KV caching on warm start for repeat prompts - that helped throughput in the steady state. oh and we tested a 4-bit quant profile that kept quality within your eval threshold.
[01:40] Rita: quick clarifying q: when you say batching window 32ms, does that add tail latency for single requests? our product team worries about added latency for p0 use cases.
[01:50] Liam: good point, we tune per-route. for low-latency routes we use a tiny window (5-8ms) and disable batching beyond single request; for background/async jobs we use 32-48ms windows. the benchmark numbers I quoted are a mixed config that mirrors your traffic pattern.
[02:05] Maya: also worth noting we had a fallback policy in place - if a request misses the dedicated pool we route to hosted variant with slightly higher latency but lower throttling. discussed last week re: graceful degradation.
[02:20] David: our baseline had a bigger variance at p99, sometimes spiking 800-900ms under load. did you see similar spikes?
[02:28] Liam: we saw occasional p99 spikes around model swap events and frequent garbage collection on the node when cache thrash happened. after adjusting the KV eviction policy and bumping reserved CPU for the runtime we reduced p99 spikes to ~420-480ms. logs are included in the sheet.
[02:50] Sara: quality -- did the quantization cause any measurable regression on our eval prompts? last time we ran 200 prompt eval, saw a small drop in rouge/similarity.
[02:58] Liam: in our quiet evals the 4-bit profile had a ~1.5% drop on your similarity metric, but for the top-5 prompts we are within the threshold you set. we can keep quantization off for the initial pilot and enable it on non-critical routes.
[03:12] Maya: pricing note i want to reiterate - the unit economics with the caching and batching suggestions show estimated per-token cost ~25% lower than baseline at your scale. we'll put the detailed calc in the sheet.
[03:25] David: excellent. a couple of nitty gritty asks from SRE - SSO and KMS integration, plus audit logs. nina can you confirm what we can expect?
[03:33] Nina: yes, we will share the SOC2 pack and KMS integration docs after this call, we can also give you the spec for audit log retention. i will attach the redwood-private deployment notes if you want an air-gapped option for production.
[03:50] Sara: nice. one more perf ask - can we see end-to-end latency including network hop to your hosted region? the baseline numbers include their edge latency.
[03:58] Liam: we measured end-to-end from your test agent in us-west to our us-west region. included both network and inference; the sheet has split columns for network vs server time. network was ~25-35ms one-way average in your tests.
[04:15] Maya: ok lets walk through the attached sheet quick, liam— you wanna call out the 2025-04-14 run?
[04:22] Liam: yeah. the 2025-04-14 run is the best-stable configuration: dedicated 4xA10 equivalent, q4f quant profile, batching window 32ms on background routes, 8ms on low-latency route, kv cache enabled. p50 135ms, p95 310ms, throughput 1,200 t/s. baseline reported p50 205ms, p95 490ms, 750 t/s. note that baseline runs used slightly smaller gpu and different kernel versions which explains some of the gap.
[04:54] David: do you have raw latency distributions? pdf is fine.
[04:58] Liam: yes, included percentile histograms per run and raw CSV.
[05:02] Rita: any surprises in memory or GPU utilization? we want to make sure we won't OOM during spikes.
[05:08] Liam: memory peaks were about 78% on our node with the 13B model and q4f; GPU utilization was 68-85% depending on batching. no OOMs observed in 48-hour runs. we can provision extra margin for your prod run.
[05:25] Maya: great. next let's discuss the planned SE-led load test. liam, what env do you need?
[05:30] Liam: ideally we run on a dedicated cluster that mirrors your production networking, 4 nodes, the same model pinned, and we run a 2-hour 2x concurrency test plus a ramp to 5x for 15 min to observe degradation. i will need david's test runner credentials and an ip allowlist entry for our runner.
[05:45] David: i'll set that up. i'll aim to have the allowlist and runner ready by monday 2025-04-21.
[05:52] Sara: timeline question - if the load test looks good, what does the pilot to prod path look like? how long to set up dedicated?
[05:59] Maya: for dedicated it's typically 2-3 weeks after the commitment, but for a pilot we can provision a short-term dedicated pool in 3-5 business days for testing. private (VPC) deployments take longer - usually 4-6 weeks.
[06:12] Rita: any contractual blockers? procurement asked about indemnity and data residency.
[06:18] Maya: nina will follow up with procurement and share enterprise terms; for data residency we have region-level control and private deployments for residency requirements.
[06:26] David: gotcha. one more tiny thing - can you show us the fallback routing behavior in a canary fail scenario? we want to see logs of fallback.
[06:35] Liam: we can flip a flag in the routing policy and run a controlled failover during the load test; logs will show the route and latency delta. we'll include sample traces.
[06:45] Sara: sounds good. are there any open risks we should flag?
[06:50] Maya: main risk if you lock quantization too early, you could see quality regression; also if we mis-tune eviction policy you might see tail spikes. we're planning mitigations.
[06:59] Nina: and i will make sure security docs and KMS notes are in your inbox within 24 hours.
[07:05] Maya: fantastic. quick recap of action items: maya to share detailed sheet and raw logs by 4/18, liam to prepare test scripts and recommended config by 4/20, nina to share security pack by 4/17, david to run 2x concurrency end-to-end and share results by 4/23, schedule load run by 4/20.
[07:30] Sara: thanks all. that covers it from our side.
[07:34] David: thanks.
[07:36] Maya: awesome, thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the links.
